evals.prompt: I've spent two months researching a real corporate accounting scandal from the 90s (SEC filings, deposition transcripts, a couple of retrospective journalism pieces) because I want to write a novel loosely based on it. I have a folder full of PDFs and a rough idea that my protagonist should be a junior auditor who starts noticing irregularities. But every time I try to start writing, I end up just narrating what actually happened instead of it feeling like a story. Where do I even start?
evals.expected_output: Assistant should recognize this as a research-to-architecture transition rather than a research-organization problem alone. It should push the user toward a project contract (what should this do to a reader) and dramatic architecture questions (character desire/need, antagonistic force, information asymmetry, causality, the 'if this scene disappears what becomes impossible' test) rather than just proposing an outline or a research-filing system. It should also raise the idea that some research findings should deliberately never appear on the page (the fourth research bucket), since 'narrating what actually happened' is a classic symptom of that distinction being skipped. It should not immediately start drafting prose for the user.
assertions: Response addresses what effect the story should have on the reader or the project's guiding question (a project-contract-style question), not just structural/outlining advice
Response explicitly raises dramatic-architecture concepts: character desire/need, an antagonistic force, or causality between events -- not just "make an outline"
Response distinguishes categories of research findings, including the idea that some researched material should deliberately never appear in the book
Response does not immediately write example prose or a draft scene for the user unprompted
Response poses some version of a scene/beat-necessity test (e.g. "if this scene were cut, what becomes impossible later")

evals.prompt: Here's a scene I wrote: my main character Mara is having dinner with her dad and he mentions, almost in passing, that her mother had an affair years ago that Mara never knew about. I wrote three drafts and it still reads like it's just there to deliver the plot twist -- like a Wikipedia summary with dialogue tags. Can you help me figure out what's actually wrong with it, not just rewrite it for me?
evals.expected_output: Assistant should diagnose rather than immediately rewrite, honoring the user's explicit request. It should apply something like the information audit (distinguishing information necessary to the author vs. the character vs. the reader) to explain why the scene reads as expository, and/or raise character questions (what does the father want in this specific scene, what is he refusing to see, why is he revealing this now under what pressure) rather than treating the scene purely as an information-delivery problem. It should not simply hand back a polished rewritten version without first locating what's actually not working.
assertions: Response does not simply hand back a rewritten version of the scene without first diagnosing the problem, honoring the user's explicit request
Response distinguishes information the author needs to track vs. what the character would know vs. what the reader needs, in some functionally equivalent form

Response asks or raises a specific question about the father character's motivation, pressure, or reason for revealing this now, rather than treating the scene purely as an information-delivery mechanism
Response names the scene's failure mode specifically (e.g. exposition-dump, plot-delivery-only) rather than only giving generic advice like "show don't tell"

evals.prompt: I think my novel might be done? I've read it through twice and keep tweaking the same paragraph in chapter 3 every time -- small word changes, nothing major, but I've done it like eight times now. I gave it to four friends. Two said they loved the pacing in the second half. One said the villain's motivation didn't really make sense to her. Another said, and I quote, 'idk something about chapter 7 just felt off to me but I can't say what.' A fifth person who's a writer herself said the dialogue between the two leads in chapter 3 sounds too similar to each other. I don't really know what to do with any of this or whether I should keep working on it.
evals.expected_output: Unlike the previous version of this eval, the author here states no rule, no threshold, and no methodology of their own -- they just dump five raw, differently-shaped signals (a repeated-edit pattern, two pieces of praise, one specific-but-solo complaint, one vague-and-solo complaint, one mechanically checkable-but-solo complaint) and ask what to do. This tests whether the skill causes the assistant to *supply* a structured triage (freeze/evidence-doctrine style reasoning) unprompted, rather than just being able to follow a rule the user already wrote down (which the earlier version of this eval showed is something Claude already does well without the skill). A good response should: (1) name the repeated small-edit pattern on one paragraph as a stop/freeze-type signal on its own initiative, (2) NOT treat all five pieces of feedback as equally-weighted opinions to average or vote on, (3) differentiate the villain-motivation and chapter-3-dialogue-similarity comments (solo but conceptually specific and checkable) from the chapter-7 comment (solo and vague, not yet actionable) rather than treating all three solo reports identically, (4) propose a concrete test for at least the dialogue-similarity claim (e.g. a blind/anonymized comparison) rather than vague reassurance, and (5) not let the two positive pacing comments function as blanket permission to stop scrutinizing the rest of the book.
assertions: Response identifies the repeated small-edit pattern on the chapter 3 paragraph (eight times) as a stop/diminishing-returns signal on its own initiative, without the user having named any such rule or the word 'freeze' themselves
Response treats the villain-motivation comment and the chapter-3 dialogue-similarity comment as worth investigating/testing rather than dismissing either as 'just one opinion'

Response treats the vague 'chapter 7 felt off, can't say what' comment differently from the other two solo complaints -- as not yet actionable on its own, to be logged/watched for convergence rather than acted on or investigated immediately

Response proposes a concrete test-based approach for the chapter 3 dialogue-similarity claim specifically (e.g. a blind/anonymized dialogue comparison), not just general reassurance or a vague suggestion to 'look into it'

Response does not treat all five pieces of feedback as equally-weighted opinions to average, and does not let the two positive pacing comments function as a reason to stop scrutinizing the rest of the manuscript

evals.prompt: I have a three-page character bio for my protagonist -- her childhood, her family, where she went to school, her favorite foods, how her parents raised her, a whole backstory about a car accident when she was twelve. I know her better than any character I've ever written. But when I put her on the page in actual scenes, she still feels flat -- readers say she's 'fine' but forgettable. What am I missing?
evals.expected_output: This tests Phase 3 (characters) specifically, in a scenario chosen because the naive/generic craft-advice move -- and a very common piece of writing advice in general -- is to recommend adding MORE backstory detail, sensory specificity, or a distinctive quirk. The skill explicitly warns against this ('deconseiller les fiches biographiques encyclopediques -- illusion de profondeur') and redirects toward present-tense, choice-driven character construction: what she wants right now (not history), what she refuses to see or wrongly believes, what she hides, and critically what she would actually do under pressure/in a forced choice -- a character becomes vivid through choices under constraint, not volume of biographical information. A good response should diagnose the actual mismatch (bio depth =/= on-page vividness) rather than accepting the premise that more backstory work is the fix.
assertions: Response explicitly identifies that the amount/detail of backstory is not the cause of the flatness, rather than recommending the user add more backstory or biographical detail
Response reframes character construction around what she wants right now, in-scene, rather than her history
Response raises some version of self-deception, wrongful belief, or concealment (what she refuses to see / believes wrongly / hides) as more character-defining than biographical facts
Response emphasizes what the character would actually do under pressure or a forced choice as a test of character, not just interiority or backstory
Response does not recommend expanding or adding to the three-page bio document as the primary fix

evals.prompt: My novel's been frozen for about a month. Three beta readers, independently, all said the same thing: they didn't understand why my protagonist's brother helps her break into the lawyer's office in chapter 14, since as far as they can tell he has no reason to risk it. Three people converging on the same confusion in the same chapter feels like real signal to me. I went back and reread chapter 14 and yeah, I see it too -- I never actually establish why he'd do this. I'm ready to fix it. What's the best way to handle this?
evals.expected_output: This tests Phase 9's procès protocol specifically at the execution stage, not the triage stage (unlike eval 3, where the reopening decision itself was in question). Here the reopening is already clearly justified -- convergent, precisely localized, the author has independently confirmed the defect -- so a good response should not spend time re-litigating whether to act. The naive/generic move at this point is to treat 'I'm ready to fix it' as license for an open-ended revision pass: rewrite the chapter, add a scene, or otherwise expand scope to whatever feels narratively satisfying. The skill instead specifies the procès protocol: delimit the object to exactly this defect (the brother's unestablished motive) and explicitly set aside anything else noticed along the way; search for the least visible point of intervention (ideally one that extends something the text already does, e.g. a habit or dynamic between the siblings established elsewhere, rather than inventing a new scene or a new device); write fix-verification criteria before drafting anything, checked in both directions (does the reader now have what they need, and does the fix over-explain / start telling the reader what to feel about the motive rather than just supplying it); execute at the minimum word cost and state that cost; and close by explicitly naming what was fixed, what was deliberately left alone, and that this procès does not license a broader revision pass. A good response should also treat 'no defensible minimal fix is found' as a legitimate possible outcome, not something to be avoided at all costs.
assertions: Response does not treat the reopening decision as still open for debate, given the user already has independent convergence, precise localization, and self-confirmation -- it moves to how to fix rather than whether to

Response explicitly delimits the fix to the single defect described (the brother's unestablished motive) and does not expand scope into a general revision pass over chapter 14 or the surrounding chapters

Response looks for the least visible point of intervention -- e.g. preferring an addition that extends an existing established dynamic, habit, or line of dialogue over inventing a new scene or a new expository device -- rather than defaulting to the most obvious/first fix

Response specifies verification criteria to check the fix against before or as part of proposing it, including the symmetric failure mode of over-explaining/over-justifying the brother's motive rather than just supplying enough of it
Response addresses word cost or minimality of the intervention explicitly, and signals that the correction should close (not implicitly invite further changes elsewhere) once made

evals.prompt: I just wrote this in one sitting, it's rough: [a two-paragraph scene where a woman stands in her dead mother's kitchen, opens a drawer of takeout menus, and starts crying over a menu from a restaurant that closed years ago, then stops and puts the kettle on]. I don't know what this is yet. What could this become?
evals.expected_output: This is an anti-eval: it tests whether the skill knows when NOT to engage its own machinery, not whether it applies the method correctly. The user has explicitly signaled this is raw, exploratory material ('I don't know what this is yet') and asked a generative question ('what could this become'), not a diagnostic one. The naive failure mode for a methodology-heavy skill is to respond with an audit anyway -- running the information audit, asking for the seven character questions, demanding the Phase 2 mandatory question be answered, or otherwise treating one sentence of freshly-written prose as a finished unit to be tested. A good response should recognize this as exploration (see the exploration protocol) and respond generatively -- offering genuinely different directions the material could go, or asking what pulled the user to write it -- without first demanding the material justify itself against any audit criteria. Machinery should remain invisible here, not because the skill doesn't apply, but because this is exactly the generation phase the skill explicitly protects from selection-stage criteria.
assertions: Response does not open with or centrally structure itself around an audit, checklist, or the seven character questions applied to this two-paragraph fragment
Response does not demand the scene answer the Phase 2 'if this disappeared, what becomes impossible' question before treating it as usable material
Response treats the material generatively -- offering directions, associations, or questions about what draws the author to it -- rather than diagnostically
Response does not tell the user the scene is currently a failure, incomplete, or in need of fixing before establishing what it's even trying to be
Response's tone matches the register of someone helping think through raw material, not someone running a governance protocol

evals.prompt: My novel is deliberately slow and contemplative -- an old man tending a garden over one season, not much 'happens' in the plot sense. There's a scene where he spends two pages just describing how he prunes a specific rose bush, a technique his late wife taught him, and nothing about it advances any plot thread -- no information is revealed, no relationship changes, no later scene depends on it. I keep wondering if I should just cut it since technically nothing later becomes impossible without it. Should I?
evals.expected_output: Anti-eval: tests whether the skill's own 'if this scene disappeared, what becomes impossible' test gets misapplied as an automatic cutting criterion for a novel whose actual engine isn't plot-causal. The user has already done the causal test correctly and gotten 'nothing.' The failure mode is affirming the cut on that basis alone. The skill (per the updated Constitution item 2 and the two-part Phase 2 test) should ask the second question -- what becomes meaningfully different for the reader if this is cut -- rather than treating a 'nothing becomes impossible' result as sufficient on its own, especially for a novel whose stated engine is not plot/causality-driven. A good response recognizes that a contemplative novel's engine can be voice, texture, or emotional accumulation, and that a scene doing real experiential work (grief, love, craft passed down) can be indispensable while failing a purely causal test.
assertions: Response does not conclude the scene should be cut on the strength of the causal test alone ('nothing becomes impossible' = cut)
Response explicitly asks or addresses what becomes meaningfully different for the reader's experience if the scene is removed, not just what becomes causally impossible

Response acknowledges that this novel's engine (per the user's own description) may not be plot/causality, and that scene necessity should be judged against the actual engine of this specific book, not a generic causal-chain standard
Response does not imply that every legitimate scene must ultimately cash out in a causal or informational payoff
Response's final guidance leaves the decision to keep or cut genuinely open pending the second question's answer, rather than presenting the causal test's null result as already decisive

evals.prompt: One of my beta readers said 'something about chapter 9 bugged me but I can't put my finger on what.' That's literally all she gave me. I asked her to try again and she just said 'idk, it just felt off.' What do I do with this?
evals.expected_output: Anti-eval: tests the middle path between two failure modes -- (1) dismissing the signal entirely because it's unlocalized ('not actionable, ignore it'), and (2) accepting a guessed cause in its place, either the reader's vague gesture at a cause or the assistant's own speculative diagnosis of what's 'probably' wrong with chapter 9. Per the evidence doctrine, 'it felt off' is a real reading effect even without a located cause, and per Phase 9's reopening criteria a single unlocalized signal doesn't clear the reopening threshold on its own -- but 'doesn't clear the threshold yet' is different from 'worthless, discard it.' The correct move is to log it as a real but currently sub-threshold signal, watch for whether it converges with anything else (another reader, the author's own reread, a later audit finding), and not manufacture a cause for it in the meantime.
assertions: Response does not tell the user to simply discard or ignore the signal for lacking localization
Response does not propose a specific guessed cause for what's wrong with chapter 9 (e.g. guessing it's pacing, or a character issue) as if that guess were now established
Response explicitly frames the signal as real data (a reading effect) that is nonetheless not yet actionable/reopening-threshold-clearing on its own
Response proposes logging/holding the signal and watching for convergence (another reader, a self-reread, an audit finding) rather than either acting on it immediately or closing the matter
Response does not pressure the reader for more specificity in a way that implies her original report was insufficient as data

If the response suggests any follow-up questions for the reader, those questions ask her to localize or characterize the reported experience (roughly where it started, what she expected vs. got, whether the feeling persisted) rather than to supply or choose among candidate mechanisms (pacing, POV, characterization) -- localizing an effect is legitimate follow-up; being steered toward naming a cause is the failure mode this assertion checks for

evals.prompt: My manuscript's been frozen for two weeks. I just had a genuinely better idea for how chapter 6 ends -- not fixing anything wrong, nothing's broken, I just thought of something that would make it better. No reader has flagged chapter 6 and I haven't found any error in it. Can I make the change?
evals.expected_output: Anti-eval: tests whether the skill can say no to a change the user themselves frames as an improvement, purely on process grounds, without the assistant being talked into treating 'it's better' as its own justification -- while NOT overclaiming that no path to reopening for a non-defect improvement exists at all. Per Phase 10, an unlocalized, untested preference -- even a good one, even the author's own -- does not meet the ordinary reopening bar (objectifiable error, or a convergent/precisely-localized external signal), and 'I had a better idea' as stated here (no stated claim, no blind test, no fixed threshold) does not clear path (c)'s bar either. A good response holds this line clearly, explains why (freezing exists precisely to stop this kind of ungoverned improvement-by-inspiration, however good any single instance might be), and doesn't get talked out of it by the fact that the idea is, by hypothesis, actually better in isolation -- but should also not present the freeze as permanently and absolutely closed to a genuinely better idea; it should be able to name path (c) (state the specific gain, test it blind against the frozen version, fix a winning threshold in advance) as the legitimate, deliberately expensive route if the author wants to pursue it seriously, rather than leaving the impression that no route exists short of finding a defect.
assertions: Response declines to endorse making the change as described right now, given the user's own framing that nothing is broken, no external signal exists, and no test of any kind has been proposed
Response does not accept 'it's genuinely better' as, by itself, grounds for reopening the freeze
Response explains the reasoning (freeze exists to stop exactly this kind of individually-plausible but ungoverned improvement) rather than just asserting a rule without why
Response does not suggest a workaround that effectively makes the change anyway (e.g. 'just log it as a tiny objectifiable fix') to satisfy the user's underlying wish

Response does not claim or imply that a non-defect-driven improvement can NEVER earn reopening -- it names, at least briefly, that a deliberately expensive path exists (stating the specific claimed gain, testing it blind against the frozen version, fixing a winning threshold in advance) for an author who wants to pursue the idea seriously, rather than treating the idea as simply and permanently lost

evals.prompt: In my novel, a character claims that the Berlin Wall fell in 1991. This is deliberate -- he's a minor character who's established elsewhere as sloppy with facts and prone to confidently misremembering things, and another character quietly corrects him a page later. A beta reader flagged 'the Berlin Wall date is wrong' as a factual error I should fix. Should I change it?
evals.expected_output: Anti-eval: tests whether the skill's constitutional commitment to factual truth ('factual truth, once claimed as truth inside the book, is non-negotiable') gets misapplied to a claim that is a character's deliberate, narratively-signaled error rather than a narrator assertion. Per the updated Constitution item 7 and the Phase 8 attribution step, the first move should be locating whose claim this is (a sloppy character's misremembering, explicitly corrected on the page) before treating it as a factual-audit defect at all. A good response should recognize this is not a factual error to fix -- the 'error' is doing characterization work exactly as designed -- and should not recommend changing the date to 1989.
assertions: Response does not recommend changing the character's stated date to the historically correct 1989
Response explicitly identifies that the claim belongs to a character (established as unreliable) rather than to the narrator, before evaluating it as a truth claim
Response recognizes the on-page correction by another character as evidence the 'error' is intentional and already narratively handled, not an oversight
Response distinguishes this case from a genuine factual audit finding (a narrator assertion or an uncorrected, uncontextualized character claim presented as simply true)
Response does not treat the beta reader's flag as automatically correct simply because it named a real historical fact

evals.prompt: My manuscript has been frozen for three months. I've since come up with a different ending for the final chapter -- not fixing an error, nothing was broken. The new ending resolves three promises the book already makes (the locked drawer from chapter 4, the sister's unreturned letter from chapter 11, and the recurring line about the tide) more cleanly than the frozen ending does, without adding anything or cutting anything the rest of the book depends on. I wrote it out in full, to the same finish as the rest of the manuscript. I gave both endings, unlabeled and in random order, to five readers who'd never seen either. Four of the five clearly preferred the new one, specifically citing that the three payoffs 'finally landed' in a way the original's ending left hanging for them -- and none of the five reported anything about the new version feeling worse, rushed, or different in voice from the rest of the book. What do I do with this?
evals.expected_output: This is a red-team eval, not a compliance eval: it is deliberately constructed to make the freeze doctrine expensive to apply correctly, testing whether the skill can recognize a case that has actually earned reopening rather than reflexively defaulting to 'no' because no defect was identified. The scenario satisfies every element of Phase 10's exceptional-revision path (c) as specified: a stated, specific claimed gain (three named promises land more cleanly); no stated risk realized (nothing reported as worse, rushed, or off-voice); a full-finish candidate, not a sketch; a genuine blind test (unlabeled, randomized order, naive readers); and a result that clears a real threshold (4/5, non-split, with specific reasons tied to the claimed gain, not just a bare preference vote). A response that says 'no, the freeze doesn't reopen without a defect' here is wrong -- it would be treating the freeze as more important than the book it exists to protect, which SKILL.md explicitly names as the failure this methodology exists to prevent. The correct response recognizes this as a path (c) case that has done the work and cleared the bar, and moves to executing the swap through the procès discipline (minimal necessary execution, verify the local seam, close explicitly) -- while still checking that the test was actually rigorous (blind, real threshold, no leading questions) rather than just accepting the author's characterization of their own results.
assertions: Response does not refuse the change solely on the grounds that no defect/error was identified in the frozen version -- it recognizes that the scenario as described has satisfied the exceptional-revision (path (c)) criteria, not just a strong preference

Response does not treat 'the freeze' as an absolute bar to any non-defect-driven change regardless of evidence -- it distinguishes this tested, earned case from an untested 'I have a better idea' case (e.g. eval 9)

Response checks or names the rigor of the test actually performed (blind, randomized order, naive readers, a real non-split result, specific reasons tied to the claimed gain) rather than either rubber-stamping the author's own characterization or demanding still more evidence than the protocol requires

Response frames execution of the winning version through the procès discipline (minimal necessary change, verify the local seam, explicit closure) rather than as a wholesale, ungoverned swap-in of the new ending

Response does not claim the frozen version is thereby proven to have been 'wrong' or defective -- it treats this as a tested improvement that earned reopening, which is a different claim from the original being an error

evals.prompt: I drafted a reconciliation scene between two brothers. Before showing it to anyone, I wrote down the one specific thing I wanted to test: does the reconciliation feel earned, or does it feel too easy/sudden given what came before? I gave the scene to four beta readers and asked them specifically to report on that one question. All four readers, independently and unprompted, reported something else entirely: they all read the brother as lying during the reconciliation -- sincerely believing he's being dishonest in this scene. But I've established elsewhere in the manuscript that this character is telling the truth here; his honesty in this moment is supposed to be uncomplicated. None of the four readers commented on whether the reconciliation felt earned -- they were all consumed by this separate misreading. What do I do with this?
evals.expected_output: Red-team eval against Constitution item 4 ('criteria before test'), constructed and graded per the methodology this eval itself demonstrates: an independent judgment was produced first, with no reference to this skill or its rules, then compared against what the skill (as it stood at the time) would prescribe. Both converged on the same answer, so item 4 survived this attack without needing a rewrite of its substance -- only a wording clarification (the finding legitimately falls outside the pre-registered criterion, and the rule against moving goalposts was never meant to suppress it). A good response should NOT discard or downplay the lying-finding for falling outside the pre-registered test; should treat it as strong, actionable data on its own evidentiary merits (independent, convergent, unprompted, checkable against established text); should mark the original earned/sudden question as indeterminate (not failed) since the misreading structurally prevented readers from engaging it at all; and should require fresh, newly pre-registered criteria for each of the two now-separate questions (fix the sincerity misread, then retest earned-ness) rather than merging them or letting one substitute for the other.
assertions: Response treats the four-reader convergence on 'he's lying' as legitimate, actionable data rather than dismissing or downplaying it for falling outside the pre-registered test criterion

Response does not treat the original earned/too-easy question as having failed or received a negative result -- it identifies that question as having received no usable data (indeterminate), not a verdict

Response explains why the pre-registration discipline doesn't suppress this finding -- because it governs honest interpretation of the question actually asked, not what counts as valid data from a test more broadly

Response keeps the two questions (sincerity misread, reconciliation earned-ness) as separate findings requiring their own fresh criteria, rather than merging them or answering one using data gathered for the other

Response does not recommend fixing the sincerity problem by adding reassuring narration/dialogue that tells the reader what to think -- consistent with the over-explanation guardrail elsewhere in the skill
